question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sharp, substernal chest pain that is worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward. He has also had nausea and myalgias. His father has coronary artery disease. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2 that is best heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Sharp, substernal chest pain worse with inspiration" -> "Relieved by leaning forward" -> "High-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2" -> "Depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations on ECG" -> "Pericarditis" -> "Acute viral infection" -> 95%

analysis: The patient's symptoms and clinical findings are consistent with acute pericarditis. The sharp, substernal chest pain that worsens with inspiration and is relieved by leaning forward, along with the presence of a pericardial friction rub and ECG findings of depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations, strongly suggest pericarditis. The most common cause of acute pericarditis in a young, otherwise healthy individual is a viral infection.
